```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(plotly)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))
set.seed(258)

plot_cols <- list(
  teal        = "#00695c",
  teal_dark   = "#004d40",
  teal_light  = "#e0f2f1",
  blue        = "#c8e6f3",
  blue_soft   = "#eef8fb",
  grey        = "#f5f6f7",
  yellow      = "#fff8e1",
  orange      = "#f9a825",
  red         = "#c62828",
  text        = "#2f3437",
  muted       = "#667174",
  border      = "#d8dee2",
  code        = "#f3f4f5",
  white       = "#ffffff"
)

plotly_anova_layout <- function(
  p,
  title = NULL,
  x_title = NULL,
  y_title = NULL,
  height = 340,
  margin = list(l = 64, r = 20, t = 58, b = 58)
) {
  p |>
    layout(
      title = list(text = title, font = list(size = 16), x = 0.02),
      height = height,
      margin = margin,
      xaxis = list(
        title = x_title,
        zeroline = FALSE,
        showline = TRUE,
        fixedrange = TRUE,
        linecolor = plot_cols$border,
        gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.08)"
      ),
      yaxis = list(
        title = y_title,
        zeroline = FALSE,
        showline = TRUE,
        fixedrange = TRUE,
        linecolor = plot_cols$border,
        gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.08)"
      ),
      dragmode = FALSE,
      paper_bgcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0)",
      plot_bgcolor = "white",
      showlegend = FALSE
    ) |>
    config(
      displayModeBar = FALSE,
      displaylogo = FALSE,
      scrollZoom = FALSE,
      doubleClick = FALSE,
      responsive = FALSE
    )
}
```

## Chapter Roadmap {.compact}

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">8.1 - ANOVA model</span>
Compare $k \ge 3$ population means using one global model.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">8.2 - Variation split</span>
Break total variation into treatment variation and error variation.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">8.3 - ANOVA F test</span>
Use the ANOVA table and a right-tailed $F$ distribution.
:::
::::

<br>

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">8.4 - Assumptions</span>
Normal residuals, equal population variance, and independent observations.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">8.5 - Pairwise comparisons</span>
After rejecting ANOVA, compare means in pairs.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">8.6 - R checks</span>
Use `oneway.test()`, `aov()`, and pairwise confidence intervals.
:::
::::

---

## Why ANOVA?

::: {.defbox}
**Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)** is used to compare several population means.

Suppose we have $k$ groups, where usually $k \ge 3$.
:::

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Question</span>

Do all groups have the same population mean?
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Null hypothesis</span>

$$
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\cdots=\mu_k
$$
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Alternative</span>

$$
H_a:\text{at least one }\mu_j\text{ is different}
$$
:::
::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
ANOVA starts with one global test. If the global test rejects, pairwise comparisons can then ask which means differ.
:::

---

## One-Factor ANOVA Model

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
The textbook model is:

$$
Y_{ij}=\mu+\tau_i+\epsilon_{ij},
\qquad
\epsilon_{ij}\sim N(0,\sigma^2)
$$

where $Y_{ij}$ is observation $j$ in group $i$.
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Meaning</span>

- $\mu$: overall mean
- $\tau_i$: treatment-specific effect
- $\epsilon_{ij}$: random error term
- $\mu+\tau_i$: group mean
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.defbox .fragment}
Equivalent form:

$$
Y_{ij}=\mu_i+\epsilon_{ij},
\qquad
\epsilon_{ij}\sim N(0,\sigma^2)
$$

where $\mu_i$ is the population mean for group $i$.
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
Every observation in the same group is assigned the same group mean, plus random error.
:::
:::
::::

---

## Data Structure and Notation

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.col}
| Group 1 | Group 2 | $\cdots$ | Group $k$ |
|---:|---:|:---:|---:|
| $X_{11}$ | $X_{21}$ | $\cdots$ | $X_{k1}$ |
| $X_{12}$ | $X_{22}$ | $\cdots$ | $X_{k2}$ |
| $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ | $\ddots$ | $\vdots$ |
| $X_{1n_1}$ | $X_{2n_2}$ | $\cdots$ | $X_{kn_k}$ |
| $\bar X_1$ | $\bar X_2$ | $\cdots$ | $\bar X_k$ |
| $S_1^2$ | $S_2^2$ | $\cdots$ | $S_k^2$ |
| $n_1$ | $n_2$ | $\cdots$ | $n_k$ |
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.notebox}
<span class="label">Notation</span>

- $\bar X_i$: sample mean of group $i$
- $S_i^2$: sample variance of group $i$
- $n_i$: sample size of group $i$
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
Total sample size:

$$
n=n_1+n_2+\cdots+n_k
$$

Overall sample mean:

$$
\bar X=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}X_{ij}
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{k} n_i\bar X_i
$$
:::
:::
::::

---

## Sources of Variation

::: {.defbox}
ANOVA works by splitting variation into two pieces: variation **within** groups and variation **between** groups.
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Within groups: error variation</span>

$$
SSE=\sum_{i=1}^{k}(n_i-1)S_i^2
$$

This is residual variation inside the groups.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Between groups: treatment variation</span>

$$
SSTr=\sum_{i=1}^{k} n_i(\bar X_i-\bar X)^2
$$

This captures how group means differ from the overall mean.
:::
::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
The ANOVA F statistic becomes large when between-group variation is large relative to within-group error variation.
:::

---

## Total Variation and Decomposition

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
Total variation:

$$
SSTotal=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}(X_{ij}-\bar X)^2
$$
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Decomposition identity</span>

$$
SSTotal=SSTr+SSE
$$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.thinkbox}
ANOVA compares:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\text{between-group variation}\\[2pt]
&\qquad\quad \text{vs.}\\[2pt]
&\text{within-group variation}
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
If group means are close together, $SSTr$ is small.

If at least one group mean is far away, $SSTr$ becomes larger.
:::
:::
::::

---

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

In one-way ANOVA, the total variation decomposes into which two pieces?
::::

- $SSTotal = SSTr - SSE$
- [$SSTotal = SSTr + SSE$]{.correct data-explanation="Total variation splits into the between-group (treatment) sum of squares plus the within-group (error) sum of squares: SSTotal = SSTr + SSE."}
- $SSTotal = MSTr + MSE$
- $SSTotal = SSTr \times SSE$

---

## The ANOVA Table

| Source | df | SS | MS | F-statistic |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Treatment | $k-1$ | $SSTr$ | $MSTr=\dfrac{SSTr}{k-1}$ | $F^*=\dfrac{MSTr}{MSE}$ |
| Error | $n-k$ | $SSE$ | $MSE=\dfrac{SSE}{n-k}$ |  |
| Total | $n-1$ | $SSTotal$ |  |  |

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Mean square rule</span>

$$
MS=\frac{SS}{df}
$$
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
The F statistic compares treatment variation per degree of freedom with error variation per degree of freedom.
:::

---

## ANOVA Hypothesis Test

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
Hypotheses:

$$
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\cdots=\mu_k
$$

$$
H_a:\text{at least one }\mu_j\text{ is different}
$$
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Test statistic</span>

$$
F^*=
\frac{MSTr}{MSE}
=
\frac{SSTr/(k-1)}{SSE/(n-k)}
$$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.defbox .fragment}
Under $H_0$:

$$
F^* \sim F_{k-1,n-k}
$$

The numerator degrees of freedom are $k-1$.

The denominator degrees of freedom are $n-k$.
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
The ANOVA p-value is the area to the **right** of $F^*$, because large F values mean group means differ more than expected from random error alone.
:::
:::
::::

---

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

In one-way ANOVA, what is the null hypothesis $H_0$?
::::

- At least one group mean differs from the others
- [All group means are equal: $\mu_1=\mu_2=\dots=\mu_k$]{.correct data-explanation="ANOVA tests H₀: all population means are equal against Hₐ: at least one mean differs. (Equal variances is an assumption of the test, not the null hypothesis.)"}
- All group variances are equal
- All group means are equal to zero

---

## ANOVA P-value Visual

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.notebox}
<span class="label">Right-tail reference distribution</span>

For $k=3$ groups and $n=18$ observations:

$$
df_1=k-1=2,
\qquad
df_2=n-k=15
$$

The shaded region is:

$$
P(F_{2,15}\ge F^*)
$$

In R, this is calculated with `lower.tail = FALSE`.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{r}
#| echo: false
x <- seq(0, 8, length.out = 500)
fstar <- 5.84
f_df <- data.frame(x = x, density = stats::df(x, df1 = 2, df2 = 15))
shade_df <- f_df |> filter(x >= fstar)

plot_ly() |>
  add_trace(
    data = f_df,
    x = ~x,
    y = ~density,
    type = "scatter",
    mode = "lines",
    line = list(color = plot_cols$text, width = 2.6),
    hovertemplate = "F = %{x:.2f}<br>Density = %{y:.3f}<extra></extra>"
  ) |>
  add_trace(
    data = shade_df,
    x = ~x,
    y = ~density,
    type = "scatter",
    mode = "lines",
    fill = "tozeroy",
    fillcolor = "rgba(249,168,37,0.38)",
    line = list(color = "rgba(249,168,37,0.90)", width = 1.5),
    hovertemplate = "p-value tail<extra></extra>"
  ) |>
  layout(
    shapes = list(list(
      type = "line",
      x0 = fstar,
      x1 = fstar,
      y0 = 0,
      y1 = max(f_df$density) * 0.92,
      line = list(color = plot_cols$teal_dark, width = 2.4, dash = "dash")
    )),
    annotations = list(list(
      x = fstar + 0.55,
      y = max(f_df$density) * 0.55,
      text = "p-value",
      showarrow = FALSE,
      font = list(size = 13, color = plot_cols$text)
    ))
  ) |>
  plotly_anova_layout(
    "Right-tail p-value for ANOVA",
    "F",
    "Density",
    height = 345
  )
```
:::
::::

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

The ANOVA $F$-statistic ($F = MSTr / MSE$) tends to be **large** when:
::::

- within-group variation is large relative to between-group variation
- [between-group variation is large relative to within-group variation]{.correct data-explanation="F compares between-group variation (MSTr) to within-group variation (MSE). A large F means the group means are spread far apart relative to the noise within groups — evidence against equal means."}
- the group means are all equal
- the sample size in each group is small

## Example: Campus Café Pickup Systems

:::: {.example-grid style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 0.87fr 1.13fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 10px 18px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.taskbox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.62em; line-height: 1.14; padding: 11px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
A campus café compares mean pickup wait time across three ordering systems.
Each system is used during the same lunch rush period, and the response is minutes from order confirmation to pickup.

| System | $n_i$ | $\bar x_i$ | $s_i^2$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Mobile order | 6 | 7.0 | 2.0 |
| Kiosk order | 6 | 8.5 | 2.8 |
| Counter order | 6 | 10.2 | 3.1 |

Use ANOVA at the 5% level.
:::

::: {.stat-card .calc-left style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.76em; line-height: 1.12; padding: 13px 17px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Calculation</span>

$$
\bar x=\frac{6(7.0)+6(8.5)+6(10.2)}{18}=8.57
$$

$$
SSTr=6(7.0-8.57)^2+6(8.5-8.57)^2+6(10.2-8.57)^2=30.76
$$

$$
SSE=(5)(2.0)+(5)(2.8)+(5)(3.1)=39.50
$$

$$
MSTr=\frac{30.76}{2}=15.38,
\quad
MSE=\frac{39.50}{15}=2.63
$$

$$
F^*=\frac{15.38}{2.63}=5.84
$$
:::

::: {.notebox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.61em; line-height: 1.14; padding: 10px 14px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Hypotheses</span>

$$H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\mu_3$$

$$H_a:\text{at least one mean wait time differs}$$
:::

::: {.examplebox style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.64em; line-height: 1.15; padding: 12px 15px; margin-bottom: 0; display: flex; align-items: center;"}
With $df_1=2$ and $df_2=15$, $p=0.0133$. Since $p<0.05$, reject $H_0$. There is evidence that not all ordering systems have the same population mean wait time.
:::

::::

## Example: Short-Form Video Edit Styles

:::: {.example-grid style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 0.87fr 1.13fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 10px 18px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.taskbox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.62em; line-height: 1.14; padding: 11px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
A creator compares mean viewer watch time across four video edit styles.
Each style is tested on comparable short videos from the same account, with watch time measured in seconds.

| Style | $n_i$ | $\bar x_i$ | $s_i^2$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Clean cut | 5 | 38 | 20 |
| Captions-first | 5 | 44 | 25 |
| Meme overlay | 5 | 41 | 18 |
| Story hook | 5 | 52 | 22 |

Complete the ANOVA table and test at the 5% level.
:::

::: {.stat-card .calc-left style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.76em; line-height: 1.12; padding: 13px 17px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Calculation</span>

$$
\bar x=\frac{5(38)+5(44)+5(41)+5(52)}{20}=43.75
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
SSTr &= 5(38-43.75)^2+5(44-43.75)^2\\
     &\quad +\,5(41-43.75)^2+5(52-43.75)^2\\
     &= 543.75
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
SSE=4(20)+4(25)+4(18)+4(22)=340.00
$$

$$
MSTr=\frac{543.75}{3}=181.25,
\quad
MSE=\frac{340.00}{16}=21.25
$$

$$
F^*=\frac{181.25}{21.25}=8.53
$$
:::

::: {.notebox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.61em; line-height: 1.14; padding: 10px 14px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">ANOVA table</span>

| Source | df | SS | MS | F |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Treatment | 3 | 543.75 | 181.25 | 8.53 |
| Error | 16 | 340.00 | 21.25 |  |
| Total | 19 | 883.75 |  |  |
:::

::: {.examplebox style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.64em; line-height: 1.15; padding: 12px 15px; margin-bottom: 0; display: flex; align-items: center;"}
With $df_1=3$ and $df_2=16$, $p=0.0013$. Since $p<0.05$, reject $H_0$. At least one edit style has a different population mean watch time.
:::

::::

## Check in R: ANOVA from Summary Statistics {.compact-r}

:::: {.two-col-wide style="grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; gap: 18px; align-items: start;"}

::: {.col}
::: {.notebox style="font-size: 0.58em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 8px 11px; margin-bottom: 6px;"}
<span class="label">Campus café pickup example</span>
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

n <- c(6, 6, 6)
xbar <- c(7.0, 8.5, 10.2)
s2 <- c(2.0, 2.8, 3.1)

k <- length(n)
N <- sum(n)

SSTr <- sum(n * (xbar - weighted.mean(xbar, n))^2)
SSE <- sum((n - 1) * s2)

Fstar <- (SSTr / (k - 1)) / (SSE / (N - k))
pval <- pf(Fstar, k - 1, N - k, lower.tail = FALSE)

round(data.frame(
  F = Fstar,
  df1 = k - 1,
  df2 = N - k,
  p_value = pval
), 4)
```
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.notebox style="font-size: 0.58em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 8px 11px; margin-bottom: 6px;"}
<span class="label">Short-form video edit example</span>
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

n <- c(5, 5, 5, 5)
xbar <- c(38, 44, 41, 52)
s2 <- c(20, 25, 18, 22)

k <- length(n)
N <- sum(n)

SSTr <- sum(n * (xbar - weighted.mean(xbar, n))^2)
SSE <- sum((n - 1) * s2)

Fstar <- (SSTr / (k - 1)) / (SSE / (N - k))
pval <- pf(Fstar, k - 1, N - k, lower.tail = FALSE)

round(data.frame(
  F = Fstar,
  df1 = k - 1,
  df2 = N - k,
  p_value = pval
), 4)
```
:::

:::: {.example-grid style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 0.87fr 1.13fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 10px 18px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.taskbox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.62em; line-height: 1.14; padding: 11px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
A coach tests three practice formats and records shooting-drill scores.
Each player completes the same drill after one practice format, and higher scores mean more made shots.

| Classic | Streak challenge | Leaderboard |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 18 | 23 | 30 |
| 20 | 25 | 29 |
| 19 | 26 | 31 |
| 22 | 24 | 28 |
| 21 | 27 | 32 |

Test whether the three population mean scores are equal.

$$
\bar x_1=20,
\qquad
\bar x_2=25,
\qquad
\bar x_3=30,
\qquad
\bar x=25
$$

$$
SSTr=6(20-25)^2+6(25-25)^2+6(30-25)^2=300
$$

$$
SSE=(5)(2)+(5)(2)+(5)(2)=30
$$

$$
MSTr=150,
\qquad
MSE=2,
\qquad
F^*=75
$$

::: {.notebox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.61em; line-height: 1.14; padding: 10px 14px; margin-bottom: 0;"}

Reject $H_0$. There is strong evidence that at least one practice format has a different population mean shooting-drill score.

## Assumptions of ANOVA

::: {.notebox style="font-size: 0.72em; line-height: 1.24; padding: 15px 18px; margin-top: 10px;"}
<span class="label">Assumptions</span>

<ul class="assumption-list" style="gap: 10px;">
  <li>Observations are independent.</li>
  <li>Error terms, or residuals, are Normal.</li>
  <li>All groups have the same population variance: $\sigma_1^2=\sigma_2^2=\cdots=\sigma_k^2=\sigma^2$.</li>
</ul>
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
The common variance is estimated using the Mean Squared Error from ANOVA:

$$
\hat\sigma^2=MSE
$$
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
This is why the denominator of the F statistic is $MSE$: it estimates the shared within-group variance.
:::

---

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

Which of the following is an assumption of one-way ANOVA?
::::

- The group sample sizes must all be equal
- [Independent samples from normal populations with equal variances]{.correct data-explanation="One-way ANOVA assumes independent samples drawn from normal populations that share a common variance. Equal sample sizes are not required."}
- The response variable must be categorical
- Each expected cell count is at least 5

---

## What If ANOVA Rejects?

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
ANOVA's alternative is broad:

$$
H_a:\text{at least one mean is different}
$$

So after rejecting $H_0$, we still need to ask:

**Which mean or means are different?**
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Pairwise comparisons</span>

Compare the means in pairs.

For three groups:

- $\mu_1$ vs. $\mu_2$
- $\mu_1$ vs. $\mu_3$
- $\mu_2$ vs. $\mu_3$
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
Number of comparisons:

$$
\binom{k}{2}
$$
:::
:::
::::

---

## Pairwise Confidence Intervals

::: {.defbox}
For comparing two group means after ANOVA, use intervals for:

$$
\mu_i-\mu_j
$$
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Fisher's LSD</span>

$$
(\bar x_i-\bar x_j)
\pm
t_{n-k,\alpha/2}
\sqrt{
MSE
\left(
\frac{1}{n_i}+\frac{1}{n_j}
\right)
}
$$

More power, but does not control experiment-wise Type I error.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Bonferroni</span>

$$
(\bar x_i-\bar x_j)
\pm
t_{n-k,\alpha/(2m)}
\sqrt{
MSE
\left(
\frac{1}{n_i}+\frac{1}{n_j}
\right)
}
$$

where $m=\binom{k}{2}$.
:::
::::

---

## Fisher LSD vs. Bonferroni

| Method | What it does | Tradeoff |
|---|---|---|
| Fisher LSD | Uses ordinary pairwise intervals after ANOVA | Higher power, but does not control experiment-wise Type I error |
| Bonferroni | Adjusts each interval for the number of comparisons | Controls experiment-wise Type I error, but intervals are wider |

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Least significant difference</span>

$$
LSD=
t_{\alpha/2,v}
\sqrt{
MSE
\left(
\frac{1}{n_i}+\frac{1}{n_j}
\right)
}
$$

Conclude two means differ if:

$$
|\bar x_i-\bar x_j|>LSD
$$
:::

---

## Example: Badminton Drill Accuracy Scores

:::: {.example-grid style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 0.87fr 1.13fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 10px 18px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.taskbox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.62em; line-height: 1.14; padding: 11px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
A badminton coach wants to compare three drill programs for improving serve-target accuracy.

Players trained for **two months** using one of the three drill programs.  
After the training period, each player completed the same **serve-target accuracy test out of 40**.

| Static targets | Footwork + serve | Coach-fed targets |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 19 | 24 | 26 |
| 20 | 25 | 27 |
| 21 | 26 | 28 |
| 23 | 28 | 29 |
| 24 | 29 | 30 |
| 25 | 30 | 31 |

Use a **one-way ANOVA at the 5% level** to test whether the population mean accuracy scores are the same across the three drill programs.
:::

::: {.stat-card .calc-left style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.74em; line-height: 1.12; padding: 13px 17px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Calculation</span>

$$
\bar x_1=22,
\qquad
\bar x_2=27,
\qquad
\bar x_3=28.5,
\qquad
\bar x=\frac{22+27+28.5}{3}=25.83
$$

$$
SSTr=6(22-25.83)^2+6(27-25.83)^2+6(28.5-25.83)^2=139.00
$$

$$
SSE=(5)(5.6)+(5)(5.6)+(5)(3.5)=73.50
$$

$$
MSTr=\frac{139.00}{2}=69.50,
\qquad
MSE=\frac{73.50}{15}=4.90
$$

$$
F^*=\frac{69.50}{4.90}=14.18
$$
:::

::: {.notebox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.61em; line-height: 1.14; padding: 10px 14px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Hypotheses</span>

$$
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\mu_3
$$

$$
H_a:\text{at least one population mean differs}
$$
:::

::: {.examplebox style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.64em; line-height: 1.15; padding: 12px 15px; margin-bottom: 0; display: flex; align-items: center;"}
With $df_1=2$ and $df_2=15$, the p-value is about $0.00035$. Since $p<0.05$, reject $H_0$. There is strong evidence that not all three drill programs have the same population mean accuracy score.
:::

::::

The **static targets** group is clearly centered lower than the other two drill programs.

The **footwork + serve** and **coach-fed targets** groups are both higher, and their boxplots overlap slightly. The **red dots** show the group means and make the difference in center easy to compare.
:::

## Example: Phone Case Drop-Test Costs {.phone-case-example}

:::: {.example-grid style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 0.90fr 1.10fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 10px 18px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.taskbox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.60em; line-height: 1.12; padding: 10px 14px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
A device lab tests four phone case designs. After a standardized drop test, it records repair cost.
The same testing setup is used for every design, so differences are interpreted as design-related differences in mean repair cost.

ANOVA rejects the equal-means hypothesis.

| Case | Mean repair cost |
|---|---:|
| Slim | 87.50 |
| Rugged | 113.00 |
| Wallet | 98.50 |
| Clear | 75.88 |

The ANOVA error estimate is $MSE=17.89$, with $v=28$ error degrees of freedom.
:::

::: {.stat-card .calc-left style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.66em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 11px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Bonferroni setup</span>

There are:

$$
m=\binom{4}{2}=6
$$

pairwise comparisons.

Bonferroni uses:

$$
t_{1-\alpha/(2m),28}
=
t_{1-0.05/12,28}
=
2.839
$$

For equal sample sizes $n_i=8$:

$$
SE=
\sqrt{
17.89
\left(
\frac18+\frac18
\right)
}
=
2.115
$$

Bonferroni margin:

$$
2.839(2.115)=6.00
$$
:::

::: {.notebox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.60em; line-height: 1.12; padding: 9px 13px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Question</span>

Which phone case designs have different population mean repair costs?

A pair differs if its Bonferroni interval for $\mu_i-\mu_j$ does not contain 0.
:::

::: {.examplebox style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.60em; line-height: 1.12; padding: 9px 13px; margin-bottom: 0; display: flex; align-items: center;"}
The Bonferroni margin is 6.00. So a pairwise difference must be more than 6 dollars away from 0 to be clearly different at the family-wise 5% level.
:::

::::

:::: {.two-col-wide style="grid-template-columns: 0.82fr 1.18fr; gap: 20px; align-items: start;"}

<span class="label">How to read the table</span>

Each interval estimates a difference in population mean repair cost.

If 0 is not in the interval, that pair of phone case designs has different mean repair cost.

## Visual: Phone Case Mean Repair Costs

```{r}
#| echo: false
case_data <- data.frame(
  cost = c(
    80,92,85,88,90,84,95,86,
    110,115,105,120,112,118,108,116,
    100,96,102,98,95,101,97,99,
    75,70,82,78,76,80,72,74
  ),
  type = rep(c("Slim", "Rugged", "Wallet", "Clear"), each = 8)
)

case_summary <- case_data |>
  group_by(type) |>
  summarise(mean_cost = mean(cost), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(
    lower = mean_cost - 6.00,
    upper = mean_cost + 6.00
  )

plot_ly(
  case_summary,
  x = ~type,
  y = ~mean_cost,
  type = "scatter",
  mode = "markers",
  marker = list(
    size = 15,
    color = plot_cols$teal,
    line = list(color = plot_cols$teal_dark, width = 1.5)
  ),
  error_y = list(
    type = "data",
    array = ~upper - mean_cost,
    arrayminus = ~mean_cost - lower,
    color = "rgba(0,105,92,0.65)",
    thickness = 1.8,
    width = 8
  ),
  hovertemplate = "%{x}<br>Mean cost: %{y:.2f}<extra></extra>"
) |>
  plotly_anova_layout(
    "Mean repair cost by phone case design",
    "Phone case design",
    "Mean repair cost",
    height = 390
  )
```

::: {.thinkbox}
Pairwise intervals compare **differences between means**, not the separate mean intervals shown here.
:::

## Check in R: Pairwise Confidence Intervals {.compact-r}

:::: {.two-col-wide style="grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; gap: 18px; align-items: start;"}

::: {.col}
::: {.notebox style="font-size: 0.58em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 8px 11px; margin-bottom: 6px;"}
<span class="label">Basketball drill example</span>
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

means <- c(Classic = 20,
           Streak = 25,
           Leaderboard = 30)

n <- c(Classic = 6,
       Streak = 6,
       Leaderboard = 6)

MSE <- 2
df_error <- 15

pairs <- combn(names(means), 2)

diff <- means[pairs[1, ]] - means[pairs[2, ]]
SE <- sqrt(MSE * (1 / n[pairs[1, ]] + 1 / n[pairs[2, ]]))
tstar <- qt(0.975, df_error)

round(data.frame(
  pair = paste(pairs[1, ], "-", pairs[2, ]),
  diff = diff,
  lower = diff - tstar * SE,
  upper = diff + tstar * SE
), 2)
```
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.notebox style="font-size: 0.58em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 8px 11px; margin-bottom: 6px;"}
<span class="label">Phone case example</span>
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

means <- c(Slim = 87.50,
           Rugged = 113.00,
           Wallet = 98.50,
           Clear = 75.875)

n <- rep(8, 4)
names(n) <- names(means)

MSE <- 17.8884
df_error <- 28
m <- choose(length(means), 2)

pairs <- combn(names(means), 2)

diff <- means[pairs[1, ]] - means[pairs[2, ]]
SE <- sqrt(MSE * (1 / n[pairs[1, ]] + 1 / n[pairs[2, ]]))
tstar <- qt(1 - 0.05 / (2 * m), df_error)

round(data.frame(
  pair = paste(pairs[1, ], "-", pairs[2, ]),
  diff = diff,
  lower = diff - tstar * SE,
  upper = diff + tstar * SE
), 2)
```
:::

::::

## Bonferroni vs. Fisher: Decision Guide

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Fisher LSD</span>

- Easier to calculate.
- Higher power.
- Does **not** control experiment-wise Type I error.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Bonferroni</span>

- Controls experiment-wise Type I error.
- Uses wider intervals.
- Has lower power and higher Type II error risk.
:::
::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
Textbook takeaway: Fisher LSD is simpler and more powerful, but Bonferroni corrects the multiple-comparisons problem.
:::

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

A one-way ANOVA with $k=4$ groups has a significant p-value. How many pairwise mean comparisons are possible?
::::

- 3
- [6]{.correct data-explanation="The number of pairwise comparisons is choose(k, 2). With k = 4, choose(4, 2) = 6."}
- 8
- 16

## Final Checklist

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Before calculating ANOVA</span>

- Identify the response variable.
- Identify the grouping variable.
- State $H_0:\mu_1=\cdots=\mu_k$.
- Check independence, Normal errors, and equal variance.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">After calculating ANOVA</span>

- Fill in df, SS, MS, and $F^*$.
- Use the right-tail F p-value.
- Reject only when the p-value is small.
- If ANOVA rejects, use pairwise comparisons.
:::
::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**One slide takeaway.** ANOVA compares several means by asking whether between-group variation is large compared with within-group error variation.
:::
